title-group.article-title: The Selenoproteome as a Dynamic Response Mechanism to Oxidative Stress in Hydrogenotrophic Methanogenic Communities

abstract.p: Methanogenesis is a critical process in the carbon cycle that is applied industrially in anaerobic digestion and biogas production. While naturally occurring in diverse environments, methanogenesis requires anaerobic and reduced conditions, although varying degrees of oxygen tolerance have been described. Microaeration is suggested as the next step to increase methane production and improve hydrolysis in digestion processes; therefore, a deeper understanding of the methanogenic response to oxygen stress is needed. To explore the drivers of oxygen tolerance in methanogenesis, two parallel enrichments were performed under the addition of H2/CO2 in an environment without reducing agents and in a redox-buffered environment by adding redox mediator 9,10-anthraquinone-2,7-disulfonate disodium. The cellular response to oxidative conditions is mapped using proteomic analysis. The resulting community showed remarkable tolerance to high-redox environments and was unperturbed in its methane production. Next to the expression of pathways to mitigate reactive oxygen species, the higher redox potential environment showed an increased presence of selenocysteine and selenium-associated pathways. By including sulfur-to-selenium mass shifts in a proteomic database search, we provide the first evidence of the dynamic and large-scale incorporation of selenocysteine as a response to oxidative stress in hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis and the presence of a dynamic selenoproteome.
Selenocysteine is a rare and overlooked amino acid, but proteomic data show that it is present in some species of hydrogenotrophic methanogens as a dynamic response to an increasing redox potential.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Methanogenesis is a pivotal step in the anaerobic digestion process occurring in various environments, such as soils, wetlands, and gut microbiomes, where it generates methane and mitigates accumulation of hydrogen. While it contributes to greenhouse gas emission, methanogenesis is beneficial in biogas production. Methanogens are present in highly diverse habitats, including extreme environments,1−3 but generally thrive in reduced environments and anaerobic conditions. Methanogens display varying degrees of oxygen sensitivity4−6 and are typically cultured in the presence of reducing agents, such as cysteine, thioglycolate, or FeS, that can scavenge oxygen.7

Because of this proposed redox constraint, the surprising presence of methane supersaturation in oxygenated waters has been dubbed the “methane paradox”.8 This has since been attributed to a variety of processes, such as degradation of methyl phosphonate by Pseudomonas,9 N2 fixation by Rhodopseudomonas,10 cyanobacteria,11 aerobic metabolism of methylamine,12 and also aggregates of cyanobacteria and archaea,13,14 which retained their methanogenic activity. In combination with observations of methanogens in oxic soils,15−17 this sensitivity to higher redox potentials has been scrutinized.18

In-depth genomic analysis has categorized methanogenic adaptation mechanisms to oxidative stress.19 Methanogens exhibit a range of enzymes designed to remove reactive oxygen species (ROS). These include catalases, peroxides, superoxide dismutases, nitric oxide reductases, thioredoxin,20 and rubredoxin,21 which can all directly eliminate ROS. Moreover, ferritin plays a crucial role in limiting DNA damage by binding unincorporated iron, which can otherwise produce hydroxyl radicals upon reaction with H2O2.19,22

Oxygen sensitivity has been linked with both class I (Methanobacteriales, Methanococcales, and Methanopyrales) and class II (Methanocellales, Methanomicrobiales, and Methanosarcinales) groups of methanogenic archaea.23 While both groups possess ROS-mitigation pathways, class II was often abundant in oxygen-exposed environments and contained more genes dedicated to ROS elimination, such as superoxide dismutates and thiorexodins, and DNA-damage repair.19 Analysis of environmental metadata revealed that class II genera Methanosarcina, Methanocella,15,24 and Methanothrix(17) were 9 times more abundant in oxygenated soil samples,19 although the class I methanogens Methanobrevibacter and Methanobacterium were also detected.24

Next to the usual DNA damage caused by ROS,22 methanogens are especially prone to oxidative damage as a result of their dependence upon cysteine residues. These residues play a crucial role in the active sites in metal-chelating methanogenic enzymes25 and are present in both iron–sulfur clusters and Ni–Fe hydrogenases.26,27 Because oxidative stress can irreversibly oxidize cysteine to cysteic acid,28 another potential strategy to confer oxygen tolerance involves the use of selenocysteine.29 In contrast to cysteine, selenocysteine can readily reverse its oxidative damage.30 Selenocysteine, often referred to as the 21st amino acid, substitutes a thiol for a selenol group. Although low in abundance, selenoproteins are found in all domains of life and are incorporated through an alternative translation of the UGA stop codon, a selenocysteine-specific tRNA, and a neighboring selenocysteine insertion sequence (SECIS) element in the mRNA secondary structure.31 In eukaryotes, selenoproteins, such as thioredoxin reductase and glutathione peroxidase, play a role in oxidative stress management.32 Selenocysteine has also been detected in relation to methanogenesis, where it is present in various hydrogenases.33,34 In comparison to its cysteine counterpart, selenocysteine confers different properties, such as a lower pKa and redox potential but also increased nucleophilicity and enhanced enzymatic turnover.35,36 Despite its advantages in methanogenesis, selenium utilization has only been identified in a limited number of class I archaeal genera (Methanococcus, Methanocaldococcus, and Methanopyus)34 and the Lokiarcheaota phylum,37 which is not yet linked to a ROS-mitigating class. However, the recoding of stop codons in the Asgardarchaeota superphylum suggests a potentially broader distribution in this domain.38−40

Deciphering the response of methanogens to varying redox environments and the role of selenocysteine will aid in advancing our understanding of biogeochemical cycles and enhance the design of more robust and efficient digestion and biogas production processes.41,42 Therefore, this study presents a proteomic analysis of methanogenic cultures cultivated in the presence of the reducing agent 9,10-anthraquinone-2,7-disulfonate disodium (AQDS) and without AQDS. While the oxidation–reduction potential (ORP) was monitored with probes, proteomic analysis was utilized to examine the oxidative stress response and discern selenium-associated changes in the proteome.

sec.title: Inoculum and Culture Conditions
sec.p: Fresh digestate was collected from a primary anaerobic digester with a capacity of 7500 m3 fed with organic residues and manure as substrates from the Bånlev Biogas plant (DK). The plant operated under mesophilic conditions (39 °C). The digestate was used as inoculum in a batch process and supplemented daily with a H2/CO2 gas mixture (80:20, v/v) at an initial pressure of 1.8 bar. After 1 week of enrichment at 37 °C, the digestate was transferred to mineral phosphate medium that excluded carbon sources and reducing agents43,44 and contained 5.0 g of K2HPO4, 2.5 g of KH2PO4, 1.0 g of NH4Cl, 0.05 g of KCl, 1.0 g of NaCl, 0.05 g of CaCl2·2H2O, 0.16 g of MgCl2·6H2O, 10 mL of 141 modified Wolin’s mineral solution45 (DSMZ), and 10 mL of 141 Wolin’s vitamin solution (DSMZ). To enrich for autotrophic microbial groups, such as hydrogenotrophic methanogens and homoacetogens (Figure SI 1 of the Supporting Information), five consecutive transfers were performed (every 2 weeks), using 10% inoculum, the mineral phosphate medium, and H2/CO2 (80:20, v/v) as the sole energy and carbon source. No 2,7-AQDS or other reducing agents were added during these transfers.

sec.title: Experimental Setup
sec.p: A total of 30 mL of the enriched culture from the fifth transfer was inoculated into 30 mL of fresh mineral phosphate medium, resulting in a working volume of 60 mL, in 155 mL reactors. The experimental setup included four parallel reactors, divided into two different conditions: Two reactors contained 25 mM oxidized 2,7-AQDS (95%), added once, at the start of the enrichment period, while the remaining two omitted 2,7-AQDS. Each reactor was equipped with an oxidation–reduction potential (ORP) probe (Atlas Scientific LLC, Long Island City, NY, U.S.A.) and a pH probe (Atlas Scientific LLC, Long Island City, NY, U.S.A.) for continuous monitoring of redox potential (Figure 1C) and pH (Figure SI 2C of the Supporting Information). The reactors were reflushed daily with a H2/CO2 gas mix (80:20, v/v) and pressurized to 1.8 bar. Before reflushing, the pressure of each reactor was measured (Figure SI 2B of the Supporting Information) and the headspace gas was sampled for measuring the CH4 content with gas chromatography using a thermal conductivity sensor and a Porapak Q column with helium carrier gas (Figure SI 2A of the Supporting Information).

caption.p: (A) Left, reactor setup with 0 mM AQDS (H-ORP) and redox buffered 25 mM AQDS (L-ORP), both with a H2/CO2 (80:20) headspace and likely O2 infiltration through pH and ORP probes as a result of underpressure from headspace gas consumption; right, proposed mechanism of AQDS redox buffering.56 (B) Taxonomic abundance normalized to the top 10 most abundant genera. (C) Oxidation–reduction potential (ORP) graphs of replicate (1 and 2) methanogenic enrichments grown with 25 mM redox mediator AQDS (L-ORP, orange) and enrichment without reducing agents (H-ORP, blue) during an enrichment period. Samples for proteomic analysis were taken on days 20 (a) and 21 (b). (D) Boxplots of the ORP values during the enrichment period.

sec.title: Metaproteomics
sec.p: Duplicate cultures without a reducing agent (H-ORP) and those in a reduced environment with redox mediator 2,7-AQDS (L-ORP) were sampled on days 20 and 21 of the enrichment for proteomics analysis. Cell lysis was performed with a tissue homogenizer (Covaris). Subsequent steps, including tryptic digestion, reduction, alkylation, and peptide purification, were performed using the iST kit (PreOmics). Electrospray ionization (ESI) liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry (LC–MS) analysis was conducted on a QE Orbitrap system (Thermo Scientific) employing a 120 min gradient.46

sec.title: Metaproteomics Data Analysis
sec.p: Database searching was performed against a sample-guided Genome Taxonomy Database (GTDB) r207 database47 constructed using the CHEW pipeline (github.com/hbckleikamp/CHEW). The CHEW pipeline performs an initial annotation with de novo peptide sequencing using SMSNet48 and a clustered database search against UniRef50 with MSFragger.49 Identified peptides were aligned against GTDB r207 reference proteomes with DIAMOND.50 The genera of aligned peptides are used to construct a focused database for a final, secondary search.51 This search was performed with MSFragger49 with oxidation, phosphorylation, acetylation, and pyroglutamate formation as variable modifications. To detect selenium incorporation, an additional variable modification corresponding to the mass shift between sulfur and selenium (S–Se) was included for cysteine and methionine. Matched peptides were filtered using a reverse decoy database and a 0.05 false discovery rate. Pathways related to ROS mitigation were defined by either enzyme commission (EC) numbers, Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) orthologies, or InterPro groups (Table SI 1 of the Supporting Information). Functional annotation was performed with GhostKOALA to obtain KEGG orthologies52,53 and with homology search against UniProtKB with DIAMOND50 to acquire EC numbers and InterPro groups. To identify selenoproteins absent in the GTDB, an additional database search was performed against UniProtKB reference proteomes corresponding to species identified in the search against the GTDB.

sec.title: Enrichment under Oxidative Conditions
sec.p: Duplicate cultures of enriched full-scale mesophilic digestate were incubated in the presence and absence of 25 mM reducing agent AQDS (Figure 1A), while monitoring their oxidation reduction potential (ORP) (Figure 1C) and pH (Figure SI 2C of the Supporting Information). Given that hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis is linked to the consumption of headspace H2 and CO2, methanogenesis led to reduced pressure as low as 0.43 bar inside the reactors (Figure SI 2B of the Supporting Information), which resulted in the infiltration of atmospheric air, including oxygen, at the entry points of the sensors. Oxygen infiltration was not measured directly as dissolved oxygen but was inferred from the increase in the ORP to over 50 mV (Figure 1A). The culture conditions led to a stable pH between 6.0 and 6.5 (Figure SI 2C of the Supporting Information) but high, fluctuating ORP (H-ORP). The enrichment grown in the presence of AQDS showed a more stable ORP and a lower redox potential (L-ORP) (Figure 1C). In the first days, the ORP decreased from −200 to −400 mV as oxidized AQDS was reduced to AQDSH2. Subsequently, the L-ORP culture maintained a stable median ORP of −346 and −378 mV, closely aligning with a previously described optimum for methanogenesis of −351 mV.54 Proteomic sampling occurred on days 20 (a) and 21 (b), at which both cultures had sufficiently adapted and exhibited similar methane yields (Figure SI 2A of the Supporting Information). The addition of 25 mM AQDS proved effective at generating an optimal redox environment for methanogenesis,5,54 with reduced AQDS serving as a redox buffer to lower ORP variability55 (Figure 1C). To act as a redox buffer, AQDSH– has been proposed to react with oxygen to form AQDSHO2– at neutral pH (Figure 1A), where AQDS recovery from AQDSHO2– was identified as a rate-limiting step.56 AQDS has previously been explored as an additive to promote methanogenesis at sub-millimolar concentrations,57,58 although the addition of over 20 mM AQDS required an adaptation period,59,44 which was also observed in this study (Figure SI 2A of the Supporting Information). While added AQDS served as a redox buffer to maintain a more stable ORP throughout the enrichment period, no controlled methods were implemented for oxygen infiltration. Future research should address this limitation by employing dedicated experimental setups. This may involve integration with cathodes and anodes to control the ORP, the capability to inject oxygen, and the inclusion of a probe for monitoring the dissolved oxygen content.

Although one H-ORP reactor reached redox potentials above 200 mV, well beyond the ideal redox environment for methanogenesis, the methane yield remained unaffected. This highlights the remarkable tolerance of this enrichment toward temporary oxidative stress events. Metaproteomic analysis of both communities revealed that the H-ORP condition exhibited high enrichment in Methanobacterium (68%) and Methanobrevibacter C (16%), both belonging to class I methanogens, which are classified as oxygen sensitive. It had a lower diversity in methanogens compared to the L-ORP enrichment, which, in addition to Methanobrevibacter C (39%) and Methanobacterium (30%), included more Methanoculleus (9%) and Methanosarcina (6.5%), which are part of more oxygen-tolerant class II methanogens (Figure 1C). This increased abundance of oxygen-sensitive class I methanogens in the H-ORP enrichment was surprising, although both samples retained the ability to produce methane and demonstrated highly similar functional profiles, dominated by methane metabolism (Figure SI 3 of the Supporting Information).

sec.title: Expression of ROS Mitigation Pathways
sec.p: To investigate the physiological response to oxidative stress, functional annotation was performed using a combination of EC numbers, KEGG pathways, and InterPro families (Table SI 1 of the Supporting Information). Various enzymes and protein families associated with ROS mitigation were found to be expressed, such as catalases, peroxidases, and superoxide dismutases as well as proteins linked to thioredoxin and rubredoxin (Figure 2A). Clustering of expression profiles across the two enrichments with and without AQDS showed that most ROS-mitigating protein functions clustered together and exhibited higher expression levels in the H-ORP samples (Figure 2A). In addition, these functions were grouped with selenium-associated proteins and cysteine and methionine metabolism. Pathways involved in repair of ROS damage were analyzed, including base excision repair and biogenesis of iron–sulfur proteins. However, these showed differing expression patterns, which indicates that protein synthesis might prioritize ROS mitigation over damage repair. Identified selenium-associated proteins (Figure 2C) included the putative selenium binding protein YdfZ60 and cysteine desulferase SufS, which can also act as selenocysteine lyase.61 Detected proteins involved in selenocysteine synthesis include the SepSecS/SepCysS tRNA synthase that converts tRNA-bound serine to cysteine, SelA, which converts serine aminoacylated Sec tRNA to selenocysteyl-tRNA, and translation factor SelB, which enables selenocysteine insertion by binding to the UGA codon, the SECIS element, and selenocysteyl-tRNA.60

caption.p: (A) Cluster map of expression patterns of enzymes, pathways, and protein families associated with oxygen stress. Normalized peptide spectrum matches were standardized across samples from two enrichments without reducing agents (H-ORP), grown with 25 mM redox mediator AQDS (L-ORP), and clustered on the basis of the Euclidean distance to relative shifts in expression. Higher expression is indicated by bright coloring versus dark in the case of lower expression. (B) Normalized abundance of peptide spectrum matches (PSMs) of selenocysteine compared to the abundance of phosphorylated peptides. (C) Number of peptide spectrum matches (PSMs) corresponding to selenocysteine-associated proteins.

sec.title: Presence of Selenocysteine
sec.p: Although selenium-associated proteins were identified in each sample, no selenoproteins were identified for archaea when using the UniProtKB reference proteomes as an alternative protein database. This approach solely identified bacterial selenoproteins in Acetoanaerobium, Desulfovibrio, and Rubrivivax (Figure SI 4 of the Supporting Information). To assess the putative selenium incorporations, a S–Se mass shift corresponding to the mass difference between sulfur and selenium was included as a variable modification in a proteomic database search for cysteine and methionine. The frequency of this S–Se mass shift was compared to other common protein modifications (Table SI 2 of the Supporting Information). The S–Se mass shift was observed consistently throughout both enrichments but was 2.5 times more prevalent in the H-ORP enrichment and was detected at similar rates as peptide phosphorylation (Figure 2B). The S–Se mass shift was detected exclusively on cysteine residues and not methionine. To analyze the taxonomic distribution of S–Se substitutions, the 10 most abundant genera were clustered according to their relative abundance of all peptides and their number of selenocysteine-containing peptides. Abundance values of the genera were standardized across samples to enable the clustering of abundance patterns. This revealed the underlying trends between the H-ORP and L-ORP samples, with three distinct groups (Figure 3A). Methanobacterium displayed higher abundance and selenocysteine in the H-ORP enrichment, and Methanobrevibacter A and C demonstrated an increased abundance and selenocysteine at L-ORP, while group III (Acetoanaerobium, Methanoculleus, Methanosarcina, Desulfovibrio, Acinetobacter, and Sporomusa) consisted of several genera with increased abundance at L-ORP but less variation in selenocysteine incorporation.

caption.p: (A) Clustermap of relative genus abundances in peptide spectrum matches between enrichments without a reducing agent (H-ORP) and with 25 mM AQDS (L-ORP) and the relative distribution of selenocysteine (Se H-ORP and Se L-ORP). Abundances were standardized across samples and clustered on the basis of the Euclidean distance. Brighter colors indicate points of higher positive abundance shift across samples for each genus. (B) Mean shift in relative abundance of peptide spectrum matches (PSMs), as observed in (Figure 1C), and S–Se-containing PSMs (SePSMs) between H-ORP and L-ORP enrichments.

sec.p: The observed shift in taxonomic abundances between H-ORP and L-ORP enrichments reveals significant changes in both relative peptide abundance and relative selenocysteine abundance within the two predominant methanogenic genera Methanobacterium and Methanobrevibacter C (Figure 3B). In the H-ORP environment, Methanobacterium saw a 39% increase in relative abundance compared to L-ORP, while its percentage of selenocysteine peptides increased 5-fold from 0.51 to 2.5%. Conversely, Methanobrevibacter C showed a 27% higher abundance in L-ORP accompanied by an increase in its selenocysteine percentage from 1.21 to 2.24%. This indicates that a shift in taxonomic abundance between the two major methanogens in these samples is joined by a more substantial shift in their selenocysteine incorporation levels. Increased Se incorporation could confer a competitive advantage to Methanobacterium to become more dominant at higher ORP values (Figure 1A).

Given the established importance of cysteine and selenocysteine in methanogenesis, the presence of S–Se substitutions in cysteine-containing peptides was investigated for key methanogenic enzymes of Methanobacterium and Methanobrevibacter C (Figure 4). In comparison to the overall 2% presence of selenocysteine (Figure 2B) of H-ORP samples, selenocysteine was more frequently incorporated into specific methanogenic enzymes. High average selenocysteine incorporation rates were observed for cysteine-containing peptides in abundant methanogenic enzymes of Methanobacterium during the H-ORP enrichment. Here, 67.5% of methyl-coenzyme M reductase, 67.8% of tetrahydromethanopterin S-methyltransferase, and 95.8% of formylmethanofuran dehydrogenase contained the S–Se mass shift. Comparable selenocysteine incorporation rates were found between Methanobacterium and Methanobrevibacter for the H-ORP condition (Figure 4C). The L-ORP samples retained high selenocysteine incorporation rates for key methanogenic enzymes, albeit lower than those of the H-ORP samples, highlighting the dynamic nature of these selenocysteine incorporations.

caption.p: (A) Cysteine-containing peptide spectrum matches (PSMs) of key methanogenic enzymes observed for Methanobacterium (top row, I) and Methanobrevibacter C (bottom row, II), without a reducing agent (H-ORP) and with 25 mM AQDS (L-ORP). (B) Cysteine-containing PSMs with the S–Se mass shift of selenocysteine. (C) Percentage of cysteine peptides (A) that contained the S–Se mass shift (B).

sec.title: Advantages of Selenocysteine
sec.p: Methanobacterium and Methanobrevibacter C emerged as dominant constituents in both communities, showing similar functional profiles (Figure SI 3 of the Supporting Information). A 2.5-fold increase in the ratio of selenocysteine incorporation was observed between the H-ORP and L-ORP enrichments (Figure 2B), with the highest incorporation in methanogenic enzymes (Figure 4). The H-ORP-enriched culture expressed more enzymes related to mitigation of oxidative damage along with an increased presence of selenium-associated proteins (Figure 2A). As a result of superior enzymatic efficiencies compared to their cysteine counterparts, selenocysteine enzymes have been described as supercysteine enzymes.33,35 Next to higher enzymatic activity, their oxygen tolerance29 and potential reversibility of oxygen-induced damages30 make them suitable for microaerated environments. Their increased nucleophilicity and lower redox potential36 may also assist in maintaining methanogenesis in redox conditions that would otherwise be inhibitive.62 Selenocysteine incorporation could be beneficial in anaerobic digestion processes, in which operational conditions often lead to inadvertent exposure to oxygen, which impacts efficiency.63 Selenocysteine could also be beneficial for microaeration strategies to enhance hydrolysis and methane production.41,42

In this enrichment, the increased relative abundance of Methanobacterium and Methanobrevibacter corresponded to an escalating selenocysteine ratio, indicating that selenocysteine incorporation confers a competitive advantage (Figure 4). Interestingly, the oxygen-sensitive class I methanogens (Methanobacterium and Methanobrevibacter) dominated the H-ORP environments, while the L-ORP environment had increased abundance of the more oxygen-tolerant class II methanogens (Methanosarcina and Methanoculleus). Large-scale linking of abundance to environmental metadata showed increased abundance of class II methanogens Methanosarcina and Methanocella in more oxic environments.19 However, the class I genera Methanobacterium and Methanobrevibacter have been recurrently detected in oxic soils24,64−66 and showed resistance against cycles of desiccation and oxygen exposure, along with Methanosarcina.65,67,68 These results contradict the proposed oxygen sensitivity of class I methanogens and hint at alternative oxygen response mechanisms,69,70 which could be the incorporation of selenocysteine, as reported in this study. Given that Methanobrevibacter and Methanobacterium are among the most abundant archaea in the human gut,71 their oxygen tolerance has broader implications for the localization of methanogens within the epithelium64 and adds to the importance of selenium as a nutrient for human health.72

sec.title: Selenocysteine Incorporation Mechanisms
sec.p: Although selenoproteins have been identified across all domains of life, the utilization of selenocysteine has been documented in only a limited fraction of methanogens.34,37 Recently, it has also been associated with the Asgardarchaeota superphylum.38−40 Considering the benefits of selenocysteine, it is surprising that selenium utilization is not more widespread. The presence of numerous selenocysteine incorporations combined with the absence of detected selenoproteins contradicts the stringent requirements of UGA, SECIS, and specific tRNAs. It instead suggests a more flexible incorporation mechanism. Genomes of various archaea lacking selenoproteins have been found to contain SelB-like elongation factors.73 Additionally, several cases of codon and tRNA flexibility have been documented for incorporation of selenocysteine.74−79 Methanogenic archaea exhibit the unique feature of not directly incorporating cysteine but instead relying on SepRS and SepCysS to modify phosphoserine bound to Cys-tRNA.80,81 This could imply that certain archaea use promiscuous tRNAs that can incorporate both selenocysteine and cysteine without the need for a stop codon and Sec-specific tRNAs.80,82,83 A recent observation was made in Escherichia coli, where random selenocysteine “misincorporation” occurred without the UGA codon.84 In this case, misincorporation was deemed to be random. However, in our case, the consistently high rate of selenocysteine incorporation observed in tetrahydromethanopterin S-methyltransferase in both Methanobacterium and Methanobrevibacter C suggests otherwise and could be caused by complex regulation. Follow-up metagenomic studies would be required to verify whether selenocysteine incorporation can occur independent of UGA in these methanogenic genera. Transcriptomic analysis would further elucidate the transcriptional response of SECIS elements and tRNAs to oxidative environments.

sec.title: Detection of Selenocysteine
sec.p: Including a S–Se mass shift as modification in a proteomic database search allows for the detection of selenocysteine. However, accurately mapping the presence of selenopeptides remains challenging. Because stop-codon recoding is not part of standard metagenomic approaches, they are underrepresented in popular databases, such as GTDB. The SECIS element, which can identify selenoproteins, varies across domains and can be located in both up- and downstream locations in archaea.37 As a result of its infrequent occurrence, selenocysteine is absent in homology scoring matrices, which hampers the annotation of newly identified selenopeptides. Similar to phosphorylations, standard proteomic analysis often underestimates the abundance of modifications.85 In the case of selenocysteine, its low pKa causes selenol groups to prefer a lower pH for alkylation than is employed in standard proteomic experiments, resulting in potential underdetection. However, this characteristic also provides a target for selective selenoproteomics.86,87 As a result of the natural isotopic abundance of selenium, selenopeptides have an altered isotopic distribution, which can form another target for their detection.88 Lastly, de novo sequencing of peptides could be a promising strategy because it circumvents database construction issues.89 However, because most sequencing tools rely on machine learning,90 retraining models on curated spectra containing selenopeptides would be necessary. Regardless, when analyzing methanogenic communities, we recommend the inclusion of the S–Se mass shift as a modification in proteomic database searches as a standard practice.
